title: He Has Risen: The Great Commission
summary: At dawn on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene and the other Mary come to the tomb; an earthquake shakes the ground, an angel rolls back the stone, and he tells them that Jesus has risen. Jesus himself meets them, and they worship him. The guards report to the chief priests, who pay them to say the disciples stole the body while they slept. On a mountain in Galilee the risen Jesus meets the eleven, claims all authority in heaven and on earth, sends them to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and promises to be with them always.
story:
The sealed and guarded tomb of 27:66 is where this chapter begins, and it ends the whole Gospel. Three times Jesus predicted that he would be killed and raised on the third day (16:21, 17:23, 20:19), and here the prediction is fulfilled; even his enemies had remembered it (27:63). The chapter resolves threads that run through the book. Jesus promised at the supper to go ahead of his disciples into Galilee after he was raised (26:32), and the angel and Jesus himself repeat the promise (verses 7 and 10). The Gentile Magi who worshiped the child find their answer in the command to make disciples of all nations. The devil once offered Jesus all the kingdoms of the world from a high mountain (4:8-9); now, on a mountain, the Father has given him all authority in heaven and on earth. And the name Immanuel, God with us (1:23), is answered by the Gospel's last promise, I am with you always.

Matthew has no ascension scene and no account of Pentecost. He stops with the risen Lord's command and promise, so that the story continues in the life of the church and in every reader who is taught to obey what Jesus commanded. Acts and the letters tell how the eleven went.
historical:
The resurrection is the event on which the Christian faith stands or falls, and its evidence has been examined closely by believers and skeptics alike. Several facts are widely accepted by historians of many views: that Jesus was crucified under Pilate and buried; that soon afterward his followers sincerely proclaimed that God had raised him bodily and that they had seen him; and that this conviction transformed them and gave rise to a movement that began in Jerusalem, where the burial place was known. The earliest written witness is not a Gospel but a list of appearances that Paul says he received and handed on (1 Corinthians 15:3-8), which many scholars trace to within a few years of the crucifixion; it names Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred at once, James the brother of Jesus, and Paul himself. The Gospels agree that women were the first to find the tomb empty. Josephus says that under the law the testimony of women was not accepted (Antiquities 4.219), the Mishnah exempts women from the oath of testimony (m. Shevuot 4:1), and the pagan critic Celsus, around 175, mocked the resurrection as resting on the word of a half-frantic woman (Origen, Against Celsus 2.55). Few would have invented women as the founding witnesses of a story they wanted believed.

Matthew alone tells of the guard and the bribe, and he tells it because a rival account was in circulation: this account has been circulated among the Jews to this very day (verse 15). The counter-claim that the disciples stole the body concedes that the tomb was empty, and it lasted. Justin Martyr, writing his Dialogue with Trypho around 160, says that Jewish authorities had sent chosen men throughout the world to say that the disciples stole Jesus by night from the tomb where he was laid (Dialogue 108). Tertullian, around 200, mockingly lists the rumors: the disciples stole him, or a gardener took the body away so that his lettuces would not be trampled by visitors (On the Shows 30). The medieval Jewish counter-gospel known as the Toledot Yeshu develops the gardener story. Roman soldiers who slept on watch faced severe punishment; the historian Polybius describes a sentry who failed his watch being beaten to death by his comrades (Histories 6.35-37), which is why the priests promise to satisfy the governor and keep the guards out of trouble (verse 14). A marble slab bought in Nazareth in 1878 and now in Paris, the so-called Nazareth Inscription, records an imperial edict threatening death for anyone who removes the dead from their tombs; its date and origin are debated, and whether it has anything to do with the Christian claim is uncertain.

The second-century Gospel of Peter, known from a fragment found at Akhmim in Egypt in the 1880s, expands Matthew's guard story: it names the centurion Petronius, has seven seals put on the stone, and has the soldiers themselves watch two figures bring Jesus out of the tomb. The contrast with Matthew's restraint is instructive: Matthew describes the angel, the earthquake, and the terrified guards, but no one in his Gospel sees the resurrection itself.

Matthew and Mark point to appearances in Galilee (26:32, Mark 16:7), while Luke keeps every appearance in and near Jerusalem, and John has both (John 20 and 21). The mountain of verse 16 is not named. Mountains in Matthew are places of revelation and decision: the mountain of temptation (4:8), the mountain of the sermon (5:1), the mountain of transfiguration (17:1), and the Mount of Olives (24:3). Galilee of the nations (4:15), where the ministry began, is where the mission to the nations begins.
cultural:
The Sabbath ran from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset. Matthew's opening phrase (opse de sabbatōn) can mean late on the Sabbath or after the Sabbath, but the following words, at the dawning of the first day of the week, show that he means Sunday morning. Mark and Luke say the women brought spices to finish the burial rites; Matthew says only that they came to see the tomb, perhaps because the tomb was sealed and guarded. Visiting a tomb in the first days after a death was customary; a later rabbinic tractate on mourning, Semahot 8:1, speaks of visiting the grave within three days, and Jewish tradition held that mourning was most intense in the first three days. The Mary Magdalene of verse 1 came from Magdala on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee; the other Mary is the mother of James and Joseph named in 27:56.

First-century Jews who believed in resurrection generally expected it at the end of the age, when the righteous would be raised together (Daniel 12:2, 2 Maccabees 7:9). No one expected one man to be raised in the middle of history ahead of everyone else, which is part of why the disciples were slow to believe and why their claim was so startling. The angel's appearance, like lightning with clothing white as snow, recalls Daniel's visions (Daniel 7:9, 10:6) and the transfiguration (17:2). Jesus greets the women with the ordinary word of greeting, chairete, literally rejoice. Grasping someone's feet was a gesture of homage and supplication (2 Kings 4:27), and it also shows that the risen Jesus is touchable, not a ghost. That Jesus calls the disciples who had deserted him my brothers (verse 10) is striking: the word is one of restoration.

Baptism by immersion in water was not new. Jews practiced ritual washings for purity, the community at Qumran bathed often, and John the Baptist called Israel to a once-for-all baptism of repentance (3:6, 3:11). Whether Jews already baptized converts from the nations in the first century is debated, since the clear evidence for proselyte baptism comes from later rabbinic texts. The phrase into the name (eis to onoma) is found in commercial papyri of crediting something to someone's account, and in Jewish idiom (Hebrew leshem) of doing something with reference to or for the sake of someone; baptism into the name marks a person as belonging to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. A disciple (mathētēs) was a learner who attached himself to a teacher in order to become like him (10:24-25), and in the rabbinic schools disciples learned by memorizing and imitating their master; Jesus' disciples are to be taught to obey all that he commanded, and the teacher himself promises to remain with them.
literary:
The chapter is brief and built on two scenes of commissioning with a counter-scene between them. First the angel and then Jesus tell the women to go and tell. In the middle the guards and the chief priests invent their story, a deliberate contrast between true witness and bought testimony, and a mirror of the scene in 27:62-66 in which the same leaders asked Pilate for the guard; the two guard scenes frame the empty tomb. Then Jesus commissions the eleven. Matthew uses the same pattern of words for each commission: go, tell, Galilee, there you will see him (verses 7 and 10). The earthquake at the tomb (verse 2) answers the earthquake at the cross (27:51), and the guards who were posted to keep a dead man in become like dead men themselves (verse 4).

The closing verses gather the Gospel's key words into five sentences. The word all appears four times: all authority, all nations, all that I have commanded, and always (literally all the days). Authority (exousia) recalls Jesus' teaching with authority (7:29), his authority to forgive sins (9:6), and the question put to him in the temple (21:23); now he claims all of it, in heaven and on earth, in words that echo the Greek of Daniel 7:14, where the son of man is given authority over all the nations. The passive has been given implies the Father as giver. The command to make disciples of all nations reverses the earlier limit to the lost sheep of Israel (10:5-6, 15:24), and the Gospel ends as it began, with God with us (1:23). The German scholar Otto Michel (1950) called these verses the key to the whole Gospel, and most commentators agree.

Many readers have also heard an echo of the last verse of the Hebrew Bible as it is arranged in Jewish tradition, where Chronicles comes last: Cyrus, king of Persia, declares that the LORD has given him all the kingdoms of the earth and sends God's people up with the words may the LORD his God be with him (2 Chronicles 36:23). Matthew's Gospel, which began with a genealogy like the one that opens Chronicles, ends with a greater king who has been given all authority and who promises his own presence.

The note that some doubted (verse 17) is left honestly in the text. The Greek hoi de edistasan can mean but some doubted, separating a group from the others who worshiped, or but they doubted, describing all the eleven worshiping with hesitation; both readings have defenders. The verb is the one used of Peter sinking in the waves (14:31). Jesus' response is not to wait for their doubt to resolve but to come near and speak to them all.

The risen Jesus meets the women
The guards bribed to spread a false report

doctrines.note: The tomb is empty, the angel says He has risen, just as He said, and the risen Jesus is met, touched, and worshiped (verses 6 and 9). The church confesses the bodily resurrection of Jesus as a first-order article of faith: he was raised in the body that was crucified and buried, now glorified, the firstfruits of the resurrection promised to his people.

All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me (verse 18). The crucified Jesus now holds the universal dominion that Daniel 7:14 promised to the son of man, and the New Testament describes the same exaltation as his being seated at God's right hand (Philippians 2:9-11, Ephesians 1:20-22).

Disciples are baptized in the name, singular, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (verse 19). One name shared by three, with the Son and the Spirit placed beside the Father in the rite of entry into God's people, became one of the chief scriptural foundations for the church's confession of the Trinity, as Basil of Caesarea argued in On the Holy Spirit (375).

The risen Jesus sends his followers to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to obey all that he commanded (verses 19-20). The mission rests on his authority, reaches every people, aims at obedience and not merely at converts, and is sustained by his presence to the end of the age.

Baptism is commanded by the risen Lord as the mark of entry into discipleship. Christians differ on whether it is to be given to the infants of believers or only to those who profess faith, and on its mode, but all traditions trace the practice to this command.

words.note: Egeirō, to raise, to wake, to rise. It occurs about 140 times in the New Testament, of waking from sleep, getting up, and rising from the dead. The angel uses the passive form twice (verses 6 and 7), which can be translated He has been raised, pointing to God as the one who raised him, as the apostles preached (Acts 2:24, 3:15), though passive forms of this verb are often used simply for rising. Jesus had used the same verb in his predictions (16:21, 17:23, 20:19, 26:32).

Proskuneō, to bow down, do homage, worship. It occurs about sixty times in the New Testament, thirteen in Matthew, which uses it more than any other Gospel. The Magi come to worship the child (2:2, 2:11); Jesus tells the devil that worship belongs to God alone (4:10, quoting Deuteronomy 6:13); the disciples worship him after he walks on the water (14:33); and here the women and the eleven worship the risen Jesus (verses 9 and 17). Matthew's use frames the Gospel with worship of Jesus.

Distazō, to doubt, waver, hesitate. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew: of Peter sinking in the waves (14:31) and of the disciples on the mountain (28:17). It is not the word for settled unbelief (apistia) but for divided or hesitant faith. That doubt appears in the very scene of worship is recorded without embarrassment, and Jesus commissions the doubters with the rest.

Exousia, authority, the right and power to act. It occurs about 100 times in the New Testament and ten in Matthew. The crowds marveled that Jesus taught with authority (7:29); he claimed authority on earth to forgive sins (9:6) and gave his disciples authority over unclean spirits (10:1); the leaders demanded by what authority he acted (21:23). Now he claims all authority in heaven and on earth, echoing the Greek of Daniel 7:14, where authority is given to one like a son of man.

Mathēteuō, to make disciples, or to be a disciple. It occurs four times in the New Testament, three in Matthew (13:52, 27:57, 28:19) and once in Acts 14:21. In the commission it is the one imperative; go, baptizing, and teaching are participles describing how it is done, though the first participle, having gone, takes on the force of a command in context. The aim is not only to win converts but to form learners who obey Jesus.

Ethnos, nation, people, and in the plural often the Gentiles, the nations other than Israel. It occurs about 160 times in the New Testament. Whether panta ta ethnē in verse 19 means all the Gentiles, excluding Israel, or all nations, including Israel, is debated: Douglas Hare and Daniel Harrington (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1975) argued for Gentiles only, and John P. Meier (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1977) replied that the phrase includes Israel, the view most scholars now hold. The same phrase names all the nations gathered for judgment in 25:32.

Onoma, name. It occurs about 230 times in the New Testament. In biblical usage a name stands for the person, character, and authority of the one who bears it, so that to act in someone's name is to act as his representative. Verse 19 speaks of the name, singular, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Matthew began with the naming of Jesus, whose name means the LORD saves, and Immanuel (1:21-23).

Sunteleia, completion, consummation, end. It occurs six times in the New Testament, five in Matthew, always in the phrase the end of the age: in the parables of the weeds and the net (13:39, 40, 49), in the disciples' question on the Mount of Olives (24:3), and in the Gospel's last words (28:20). The promise of Jesus' presence reaches all the way to the harvest and the judgment he described in chapters 13, 24, and 25.

christ:
The chapter shows Christ risen, worshiped, and reigning. He is raised bodily: the tomb is empty, the women grasp his feet, and he speaks and is recognized. He is the firstfruits of the resurrection the prophets promised (Daniel 12:2), and his rising vindicates everything he claimed before the high priest (26:64). He accepts worship from the women and from the eleven, worship that in Matthew belongs to God alone (4:10). He calls the men who deserted him my brothers (verse 10), fulfilling his word that those who do the Father's will are his family (12:50), and the first message of the risen Lord to his failed disciples is an invitation to meet him.

On the mountain he claims all authority in heaven and on earth, the dominion Daniel saw given to the son of man (Daniel 7:13-14), and he sends his people to all nations, fulfilling God's promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3), the promise with which Matthew's genealogy began (1:1). He places his own name, the Son, between the Father and the Holy Spirit in the one name into which disciples are baptized, a claim no prophet or rabbi could make. And he promises his abiding presence to the end of the age, fulfilling the name Immanuel (1:23). In Israel's Scriptures, I am with you is the promise of God to Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Joshua, and Israel (Genesis 26:3, 28:15; Exodus 3:12; Joshua 1:5; Isaiah 41:10); here it is spoken by Jesus in his own person. The church confesses on this ground that Jesus is Lord, truly God and truly man, crucified and bodily risen, present with his people by his Spirit, and coming again to judge the living and the dead.
interpretation:
The chapter has shaped Christian worship and mission more than almost any other. The Easter proclamation He has risen, and the Eastern Christian greeting Christ is risen, He is risen indeed, echo verses 6 and 7. The Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 1 to 10 at the Easter Vigil and on Easter Day in Year A, and verses 16 to 20 on Trinity Sunday in Year A. The triadic formula of verse 19 appears at the start of Christian baptismal practice: the Didache, around AD 100, directs that baptism be done in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in running water, or by pouring water three times on the head (Didache 7.1-3), and Justin Martyr around 155 describes baptism in the same threefold name (First Apology 61). Tertullian (On Baptism 13) cites the command of verse 19 as the law of baptism. In the fourth-century debates over the Holy Spirit, Basil of Caesarea (On the Holy Spirit, 375) argued that the Spirit, named with the Father and the Son in baptism, cannot be a creature.

Eusebius of Caesarea, in works written before the Council of Nicaea in 325, often cites the commission in a shorter form, make disciples of all nations in my name, without the words about baptism. F. C. Conybeare (1901) argued that this was the original text. Others, including Everett Ferguson (Baptism in the Early Church, 2009), note that Eusebius habitually abbreviated and blended quotations, that after Nicaea he cites the full form (Against Marcellus, book 1), and that no Greek manuscript or ancient translation of Matthew lacks the triadic formula.

The story of the stolen body had a long afterlife. Justin (Dialogue with Trypho 108) and Tertullian (On the Shows 30) knew it, the Toledot Yeshu retold it, and Hermann Samuel Reimarus revived the theft theory in the fragments Gotthold Lessing published in 1778. William Lane Craig (New Testament Studies, 1984) argued for the historical core of Matthew's guard story against the common view that it is apologetic legend. In art, Piero della Francesca's Resurrection (about 1460s, Sansepolcro) shows Christ rising from the tomb over four sleeping soldiers, Matthew's guards, a scene the Gospel itself never narrates.

The Great Commission, as the passage came to be called, drove the Protestant missionary movement. In the sixteenth century many Protestant theologians held that the command had been fulfilled by the apostles, and the Anabaptist Balthasar Hubmaier (On the Christian Baptism of Believers, 1525) argued from the order of the verse, make disciples and then baptize, for believers' baptism. William Carey's Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens (1792) opened by asking whether the commission still binds the church, and answered yes; the World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh (1910) and the Lausanne Covenant (1974) appealed to it as the church's standing charge. Modern scholarship has debated whether all nations includes Israel (Hare and Harrington, 1975; Meier, 1977) and how the ending sums up the Gospel, which Otto Michel (1950) called its key. Jewish scholars, including Pinchas Lapide (The Resurrection of Jesus, 1983), have engaged the resurrection accounts seriously, Lapide concluding that a real event lay behind the disciples' faith while denying that it made Jesus the Messiah.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles appear in this chapter. In verse 1 the King James Version's ‘In the end of the sabbath’ renders opse sabbatōn literally, while modern versions read ‘After the Sabbath’; Eusebius (Questions to Marinus) already discussed how Matthew's phrase fits Mark's timing. In verse 2 later manuscripts add that the angel rolled the stone ‘from the door’, and in verse 6 the King James Version's ‘the place where the Lord lay’ follows manuscripts that add ‘the Lord’, which Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Koridethi lack. In verse 9 the King James Version begins ‘And as they went to tell his disciples’, words absent from Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae and probably added to smooth the transition. In verse 19 some manuscripts lack ‘therefore’, and at the end of verse 20 later manuscripts add ‘Amen’, as the King James Version does.

The baptismal formula of verse 19 is found in every Greek manuscript of Matthew that contains the passage, beginning with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus in the fourth century, and in every ancient translation. The question of Eusebius's shorter citations, ‘in my name’, is set out under How it has been read; it concerns how one church father quoted the verse, not a variant in any surviving manuscript of Matthew.

Translation choices also show. The King James Version's ‘teach all nations’ in verse 19 renders the verb mathēteuō, which modern versions translate ‘make disciples of’, reserving ‘teaching’ for the participle in verse 20. ‘In the name’ (KJV, BSB) and ‘into the name’ (some translations and commentators) render eis to onoma, whose sense of belonging the second rendering preserves. In verse 17 ‘but some doubted’ (KJV, BSB, ESV) and ‘but they doubted’ (a possible rendering noted by some commentators) reflect the ambiguity of hoi de. In verse 20 ‘unto the end of the world’ (KJV) and ‘to the end of the age’ (modern versions) render the same phrase; age is closer to the Greek aiōn.

teach.big: Jesus is risen and reigns with all authority, and he sends his doubting, restored disciples to make disciples of all nations with the promise that he will be with them always.

outline.t: God acts at the tomb: the earthquake and the angel show that no seal or guard can hold the one God has raised.
The angel's message is the heart of the gospel: do not be afraid, he is not here, he has risen as he said; come and see, then go and tell.
The risen Jesus meets the women, receives their worship, and calls the deserters his brothers.
Truth can be bought off but not buried; even the enemies' story assumes an empty tomb.
Worship and doubt stand together on the mountain, and Jesus comes near to both with the claim of all authority.
The mission to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching, rests on Christ's authority and is carried by his presence to the end of the age.

teach.pitfalls:
One pitfall treats the resurrection as a metaphor for renewal or hope rather than an event. Matthew insists on an empty tomb, a touchable Jesus, and witnesses, and the church confesses the bodily resurrection as a first-order article of faith. The opposite pitfall turns Easter preaching into a courtroom exercise that proves the evidence but never meets the risen Lord; Matthew's women meet him and worship him.

The Great Commission is often reduced to evangelism alone, as though the task were finished when someone makes a decision. The single command is to make disciples, and the commission includes baptism and teaching people to obey all that Jesus commanded, which sends the reader back through the whole Gospel, including the Sermon on the Mount. It is also misused as a charter for cultural conquest or coercion; the one who has all authority is the crucified Lord, and his servants go as he went. Some preach it as a burden resting on human effort, forgetting that it begins with his authority and ends with his presence.

Teachers should not skip verse 17 or explain it away. That some doubted is part of Matthew's message: the commission was given to worshipers who were not yet free of hesitation. Finally, avoid using verses 11 to 15 to portray Jewish people as liars. The bribe is the act of particular leaders, and Matthew's own community, and the women and the eleven, were Jewish too.
teach.pastoral: This chapter speaks to grief, to doubt, and to failure. Those who have buried someone they love will hear the women going to see the tomb, and the angel's first words, Do not be afraid, and they need to hear that the resurrection is the ground of Christian hope for their dead as well. Those who carry doubt, or feel guilty for it, can see that Jesus came near to disciples who worshiped and doubted on the same mountain and sent them anyway. Those who have failed Jesus badly can hear him call the deserters my brothers. And those who feel alone in hard places, in illness, in prison, far from home, or in lonely ministry, can hold the last promise: I am with you always.

hard.q: Is Matthew's story of the guard at the tomb and the bribed soldiers historical, and what does the stolen body report show?
hard.a:
The objection is that the guard story looks like apologetic legend. It appears only in Matthew; Mark, Luke, and John know nothing of soldiers at the tomb, and in Mark the women wonder who will roll the stone away, as if no guard were there. The chief priests remember Jesus' prediction of rising after three days (27:63) when his own disciples seemed not to understand it; they approach Pilate on the Sabbath; and the soldiers are paid to spread a story that would admit they slept on duty. Many critical scholars, among them Raymond Brown (The Death of the Messiah, 1994), have concluded that the story grew up in Christian circles to answer the Jewish charge of theft, and the later Gospel of Peter shows how such a story could expand. Skeptical readers since Hermann Samuel Reimarus (1778) have also pressed the theft hypothesis itself as the simplest natural explanation of an empty tomb.

Responses come from several directions. William Lane Craig (New Testament Studies, 1984) argued that the details are less improbable than critics suppose: the prediction of rising was public enough to be known (12:40, 26:61), a temple or Roman guard was a reasonable precaution, and the story of sleeping guards makes sense as the leaders' improvised explanation. Others, while less confident about every detail, point to what the passage shows beyond doubt. Matthew says that the theft story was circulating among the Jews in his own day (verse 15), and Justin Martyr confirms that it was still being told around 160 (Dialogue with Trypho 108). A counter-claim that the disciples stole the body assumes that the body was missing; the dispute between the first Christians and their opponents was over why the tomb was empty, not whether it was. Against the theft hypothesis, historians of many views note that the disciples went on to suffer for their claim, which is hard to square with a deliberate fraud, and that theft does not explain the appearances Paul lists (1 Corinthians 15:3-8). Scholars who judge the guard story legendary may still accept the empty tomb on other grounds, as Dale Allison does (Resurrecting Jesus, 2005). Whether the guard story is historical in every detail is a question on which Christians who confess the resurrection differ; that the tomb was found empty is attested by all four Gospels and implied by the opponents' own account.

hard.q: Did Jesus give the threefold baptismal formula of verse 19, when Acts speaks of baptism in the name of Jesus and Eusebius quotes a shorter form?
hard.a:
The objection has three parts. First, the Acts of the Apostles never uses the threefold formula; it speaks of baptism in or into the name of Jesus Christ or the Lord Jesus (Acts 2:38, 8:16, 10:48, 19:5). Second, Eusebius of Caesarea, in works written before 325, repeatedly quotes the commission as make disciples of all nations in my name, without mention of baptism or the Father, Son, and Spirit, and F. C. Conybeare (Zeitschrift für die neutestamentliche Wissenschaft, 1901) argued that this was Matthew's original text and that the triadic formula was inserted later as the doctrine of the Trinity developed. Third, many critical scholars who do not accept Conybeare's textual theory still judge that the formula reflects the baptismal liturgy of Matthew's church in the late first century rather than words spoken by Jesus. Oneness Pentecostal churches, such as the United Pentecostal Church International, hold on the basis of Acts that baptism should be performed in the name of Jesus alone.

Responses begin with the evidence of the text. Every surviving Greek manuscript of Matthew that contains the verse, and every ancient translation, has the triadic formula, and the Didache, written around AD 100 and independent of Eusebius by more than two centuries, commands baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (Didache 7.1), as does Justin Martyr around 155 (First Apology 61). Eusebius's short form is best explained, as Everett Ferguson and others argue, by his habit of abbreviating and blending quotations, and after Nicaea he quotes the full formula himself (in book 1 of Against Marcellus). On Acts, many interpreters hold that in the name of Jesus distinguishes Christian baptism from John's and describes its character, not necessarily the words spoken, while others think the formula developed as the church reflected on the commission. Triadic patterns appear very early in Paul, before any Gospel was written (1 Corinthians 12:4-6, 2 Corinthians 13:14). Whether verse 19 preserves Jesus' exact words or the church's faithful summary of his commission is debated among scholars who share a high view of Scripture; the church receives it as the risen Lord's command, and the great majority of Christian churches baptize with it and recognize one another's baptisms on that basis.

observe: What does the angel tell the women to do, and what do they feel as they leave the tomb?
What story do the chief priests pay the soldiers to tell, and what does Matthew say about that story in his own day?
What four uses of the word all (including always) appear in verses 18 to 20?
interpret: Why do you think Jesus calls the disciples who deserted him my brothers?
What is the relationship between Jesus' claim to all authority and his command to make disciples of all nations?
What does it mean to baptize into the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and why might Matthew end his Gospel with this?
apply: The women left with fear and great joy at once. What would it look like for both to shape how you live this week?
Some worshiped and doubted on the same mountain, and Jesus sent them anyway. How does that encourage you to obey while questions remain?
Who in your life is someone you could help to learn and obey what Jesus commanded, and what first step could you take?
